raw_response:
I would investigate **KeeWeb with your own Docker-hosted WebDAV storage first**, followed by **Psono** and **self-hosted Bitwarden**. I cannot certify any of these as satisfying your master-password-hash rule literally from the documentation I verified. That condition needs a more precise storage check than the usual claim that a product is self-hosted or encrypts passwords.

I interpret “furryfox” as Firefox, and “no intermediary” as keeping the password-service and authentication path under your control while allowing the cloud infrastructure you explicitly mentioned.

### 1. KeeWeb plus your own WebDAV container

This is the most promising architecture for avoiding an intermediary password service. KeeWeb works with encrypted KDBX files and documents Windows and Linux desktop clients. Its official release page includes a Linux .deb package, and KeeWeb Connect lists Chrome and Firefox extensions. The desktop release evidence includes artifacts dated July 2021, before your June 2023 question. See the [official repository](https://github.com/keeweb/keeweb), [desktop releases](https://github.com/keeweb/keeweb/releases) and [extension repository](https://github.com/keeweb/keeweb-connect).

The concrete arrangement would be: run a WebDAV server in a Docker container on your cloud machine, keep the KDBX file in that server's persistent storage, and configure the desktop clients to open that file from your own server. KeeWeb's [WebDAV guide](https://github.com/keeweb/keeweb/wiki/WebDAV-Setup) documents such containerized storage. Serving the KeeWeb web application from a container alone does not supply this vault-storage component.

The [FAQ](https://github.com/keeweb/keeweb/wiki/FAQ) describes local operation and network transfer only when requested. That supports the architecture, but it does not prove that every persistent password-derived verifier in the desktop application, extension, and cache is confined to the KDBX file. Use a separate WebDAV login credential and verify the selected clients' stored state. Chrome compatibility also needs a version-specific check: the official README advertises Chrome, but a later issue snippet reports trouble with Chrome 131. That report is dated December 2024 and cannot establish a failure at your 2023 decision date.

**Verdict: promising, but verification required.** It is a composed application-and-storage solution. Confirmation that no prohibited verifier is persisted elsewhere, together with compatible browser versions, could make it a documented fit; a confirmed out-of-vault hash would rule it out under your literal requirement.

### 2. Psono, with the server and database under your control

Psono's current [download page](https://psono.com/download) explicitly lists Windows, Debian/Ubuntu packages, and Chrome/Firefox extensions. Its [architecture guide](https://doc.psono.com/admin/overview/summary.html) describes PostgreSQL and a server that can run in Docker.

Its [authentication documentation](https://doc.psono.com/admin/asvs/v02-authentication.html) states that a password-derived authentication key reaches the server and is hashed again for server-side validation. This could fit if “my vault” includes your entire self-hosted backend. It does not establish that no such verifier is persisted elsewhere in clients, and the exact configuration needed to eliminate any required intermediary service remains unverified.

**Verdict: keep on the shortlist, not yet a confirmed match.** Verify the complete verifier-storage map and required authentication dependencies. These are live documents; I have not established that the presently listed desktop offerings were available in June 2023.

### 3. Bitwarden, self-hosted

Bitwarden documents [Docker deployment on infrastructure you control](https://bitwarden.com/help/self-host-bitwarden/), [Windows/Linux desktop clients and Chrome/Firefox extensions](https://bitwarden.com/download/), and [Linux Deb-package support](https://bitwarden.com/help/getting-started-desktop/).

Its [security whitepaper](https://bitwarden.com/help/bitwarden-security-white-paper/) describes a master-password-derived authentication hash stored server-side. A statement that the master password itself is not stored does not answer your separate question about hashes. I did not verify all persistent client-side authentication state or every required external dependency for a concrete self-hosted setup.

**Verdict: a plausible conventional self-hosted option, but the strict hash-location condition is unresolved.** If any required hash storage falls outside the vault boundary you permit, exclude that configuration.

My preference is therefore to start by examining the KeeWeb/WebDAV arrangement. Before adopting any candidate, verify where its master-password-derived authentication verifiers persist. The evidence here is documentation-based, not a deployment or source-code audit, and undated live pages should not be treated as proof of what was available in 2023.
